paper_title: TimeRSI: Towards Self-Improved Agentic Deployment for Time-Series Foundation Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Time-series foundation models provide strong zero-shot forecast, but deployment for real-world applications still requires task-specific designs for model inputs and outputs. Direct inference can leave domain knowledge and recurring forecast errors unaddressed, while tailored pipelines require substantial human expertise and effort. We introduce TimeRSI, a self-improving agentic deployment system around frozen forecasting models. A coding agent translates task descriptions into executable pipeline changes. It tests each revision on historical forecasting windows and uses observed errors to guide subsequent revisions. During deployment, an adaptive selector chooses among the resulting pipelines using completed forecasts under similar conditions. Across 198 tasks on TIME and fev-bench, TimeRSI outperforms all submissions on six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Controlled comparisons support the value of feedback-guided revision over non-iterative pipeline search. Further experiments verify the generalization with different coding agents and forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/haoxin1998/TimeRSI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide strong forecasts on new datasets without taskspecific weight updates (Das et al., 2024; Ansari et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024). In real-world timeseries forecasting (TSF), effective deployment still depends on how task knowledge shapes the models inputs and outputs. For example, recurring holiday closures can inform demand forecasts, while known tidal cycles can guide ocean-current forecasts. Turning this knowledge into deployment pipeline around the model still requires substantial human expertise and effort. Code agents based on large language models (LLMs) offer way to automate pipeline development through program generation and evaluation (Jiang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2026). Two challenges arise in forecasting. First, plausible change may not improve accuracy. Calendar information, for instance, can enter through model inputs or separate predictor, and these choices can yield different results. Historical forecast errors help evaluate and refine such decisions. Second, pipeline that performs well on average may be less suitable as forecasting conditions change. We introduce TIMERSI, which applies recursive self-improvement (RSI) to deployment pipelines around frozen TSFMs  (Fig. 1)  . Our central idea is to use task knowledge to guide what to try and forecasting feedback to guide how to revise and use each pipeline. The agent edits input transformations, features, and forecast corrections while keeping the foundation models weights fixed. Specifically, TIMERSI combines two stages. Iterative pipeline improvement evaluates code revisions on historical forecasting windows and returns errors to the agent for further revision. separate set of later historical windows identifies candidates for deployment. Adaptive pipeline selection then chooses among these candidates for each new forecast using their performance under similar historical conditions. We evaluate TIMERSI on TIME and FEV-bench (Qiao et al., 2026; Shchur et al., 2026), covering 198 tasks. TIMERSI achieves the best scores among all existing submissions across six point and probabilistic forecasting metrics. Ablations show that our iterative deployment improvement outperforms non-iterative pipeline search with the same number of candidates. Further experiments show gains with different coding agents and TSFMs, while case studies illustrate how task knowledge becomes effective deployment code. *Contact us at hliu763@gatech.edu, badityap@cc.gatech.edu. sections.title:
2 TIMERSI: Self-Improved Deployment
for Time-Series Foundation Models
sections.content: TIMERSI automates two deployment decisions: how to improve task-specific pipeline and which pipeline to use for new forecast. code agent develops pipelines through repeated execution, evaluation, and revision. An adaptive selector chooses among them using past outcomes under similar forecasting conditions. The TSFMs weights remain fixed in both stages. Formally, let xt contain the observed history and known covariates at forecast origin t, and let describe the task, variable meanings, and sampling frequency. pipeline uses frozen model Fθ to forecast the next steps as (cid:98)yt+1:t+H = p(Fθ, xt; m). The agent improves p, while the backbone parameters θ remain fixed. The agent writes Python code across four stages: preprocessing, feature construction, context selection, and post-processing. On the input side, it can transform observations, encode task knowledge as additional variables, and choose which histories or variable groups the TSFM receives. On the output side, it can combine forecasts, fit auxiliary predictors, and correct systematic errors. This action space lets the agent translate task information into executable changes to the models inputs and outputs. App. gives the programming interface. Iterative Pipeline Improvement The outcome of new forecast is not yet known, so TIMERSI uses completed historical windows to evaluate pipeline changes. For each window, the system supplies the history and known covariates at its forecast origin, runs the candidate, and scores its predictions for the following steps. Earlier windows form an adaptation set for iterative code revision; later windows form selection set for choosing the deployment candidates. The loop starts from direct TSFM inference as the reference pipeline. In each iteration, the agent uses the task description and earlier results to propose and implement code revision. The system executes it on the adaptation windows and returns forecasting scores, window-level errors, and execution logs. The agent inspects this feedback to decide whether to refine its approach, combine useful changes, or try different one. All earlier code and evaluation records remain accessible, so later revisions can build on successful ideas and address errors observed in previous attempts. Task semantics guide what to try, while execution feedback guides what to change next. After the search budget is exhausted, the system evaluates the resulting candidates on the later selection windows. It retains the highest-ranked pipelines together with the reference to form deployment set P. This set provides several taskspecific strategies for subsequent forecasts. 2 Fig. 2: TIMERSI ranks first among the compared submissions across six reported metrics on TIME and FEV-bench. Labels name the frozen backbone of TIMERSI; LPTM (Kamarthi and Prakash, 2024) is appended below the dashed line when outside the top ten. See App. for metrics including WQL Skill and WAPE Skill, and full results of more methods. Adaptive Pipeline Selection pipeline that performs well on average may not be the best choice for every future window. TIMERSI therefore selects pipeline for each target variable at each new forecast origin. The selector describes the current conditions using numerical features of the recent history and reference forecast, including level changes, recent trends, and forecast shape. It retrieves similar completed windows and compares how the retained pipelines performed on them. For given target, let Nt denote the retrieved windows whose outcomes are fully observed by t. Each window receives similarity-based weight wt,s. Let ℓ(p, s) be the error of pipeline on window relative to the reference. The selector chooses the pipeline with the lowest weighted wt,sℓ(p,s) historical error, = arg minpP wt,s The selected pipeline supplies the full forecast horizon and all quantiles for that target. App. specifies the features, weights, and loss. sNt (cid:80) sNt (cid:80) . At each origin, TIMERSI runs and records forecasts from every retained pipeline. Once window is complete, the system adds each pipelines errors to its feedback history and uses them to inform subsequent choices. Pipeline code remains fixed during this stage, while selection adapts as new 3 outcomes arrive. Thus, iterative revision improves the available strategies, and adaptive selection determines when to use them.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: Data and Metrics. We evaluate all 98 tasks of TIME (Qiao et al., 2026) and all 100 tasks of FEVbench (Shchur et al., 2026), covering 111,177 and 235,039 forecast instances, respectively. Each instance is serieswindowtarget combination. Our default configuration pairs TimesFM 3.0 with Claude Code (Claude Fable 5). Following TIME, we report normalized mean absolute scaled error (MASE) and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), where lower is better. Following FEVbench, we report Skill Scores for MASE, scaled quantile loss (SQL), weighted quantile loss (WQL), and weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE), where higher is better. See App. for metric definitions and protocol details. Baselines. We compare with published results from all 32 submissions on TIME and 31 on FEVbench, covering foundation models, supervised forecasters, and statistical methods. Relative to direct inference with the same frozen TimesFM 3.0, it reduces MASE by 1.52% and CRPS by 1.61% on TIME. On FEV-bench, it raises MASE Skill by 2.79 percentage points and SQL Skill by 2.26 points. App. gives the full comparisons, including WQL and WAPE Skill. These results show that improving the deployment pipeline can improve forecasting accuracy without updating the foundation model. Ablation. Feedback-guided revision improves deployment. We compare TIMERSI with NonIterative Search, which proposes the same number of candidate pipelines and selects among them without feedback-guided revision (Tab. 1). Noniterative search underperforms direct inference on both benchmarks, whereas TIMERSI improves it. These results support revising pipelines based on forecast errors, rather than only proposing and selecting candidates. Generalization. Effective across coding agents and TSFMs. The gains extend beyond our default components (Tab. 8). With TimesFM 3.0 fixed, Antigravity (Gemini 3.8 Flash) reaches normalized MASE/CRPS of 0.637/0.532, outperforming the compared external submissions on TIME. With Claude Code fixed, TIMERSI reduces MASE/CRPS from 0.662/0.556 to 0.647/0.545 for Chronos-2 and from 0.669/0.572 to 0.641/0.549 for LPTM, whose FEV-bench MASE/SQL Skill also rises from 30.70/43.20 to 34.63/46.33  (Fig. 2)  . The Claude CodeTimesFM 3.0 combination achieves better results, consistent with the advantages of more advanced coding agents and TSFMs. Case studies. The agent translates task knowledge into pipeline changes  (Fig. 3)  : calendar features for parking, tidal decomposition for ocean currents, history-supported holiday corrections for demand, and daily-reset shape corrections for solar counters. The resulting pipelines reduce task-level MASE by 2.866.70%. The parking case also illustrates feedback-guided revision: after calendarpredictor blend increases historical error, the agent switches to calendar inputs and adds weekendtime interactions. Feedback thus guides changes in strategy, not just parameter tuning. App. provides full traces and additional examples.

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce TIMERSI to automate task-specific deployment through iterative pipeline improvement and adaptive selection around frozen TSFMs. On TIME and FEV-bench, TIMERSI ranks first across six forecasting metrics compared with competitive external submissions.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: TIMERSI relies on clear task and variable descriptions to connect numerical patterns with domain knowledge. Besides, gains on historical windows do not guarantee gains on future forecasts. This highlights the open problem, i.e., distribution shift, in time-series forecasting (Liu et al., 2024a; Kim et al., 2025).

sections.title: A Additional Related Work
sections.content: Pretrained forecasting models. TimesFM (Das et al., 2024), Chronos (Ansari et al., 2024), and Moirai (Woo et al., 2024) learn from diverse numerical series to support forecasting on new datasets. LPTM (Kamarthi and Prakash, 2024) studies adaptive segmentation during pretraining for crossdomain time-series analysis. These works develop the numerical backbone. TIMERSI addresses complementary question: how can an agent adapt the deployment pipeline around an existing backbone while keeping its weights fixed? Semantics and temporal generalization. LSTPrompt (Liu et al., 2024c) studies structured prompting for time-series forecasting. VL-Time (Liu et al., 2025) uses visual representations to support language-guided time-series reasoning. Time-MMD (Liu et al., 2024b) and TimesX (Liu et al., 2026a) provide benchmarks connecting numerical series with textual context. These studies motivate using information beyond raw target values; our agent turns task information into executable pipeline changes. FOIL (Liu et al., 2024a) addresses out-of-distribution forecasting through invariant learning. Rather than learning invariant backbone representations, TIMERSI uses completed forecasts to choose among candidate pipelines. Agent improvement. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) alternates generation, self-feedback, and revision. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) carries verbal reflections from task feedback into later attempts. GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) evolves prompts using execution traces and reflective feedback. Adaptive Auto-Harness (Liu et al., 2026b) combines harness evolution and task-wise routing on openended streams. TIMERSI focuses on executable pipelines around frozen numerical forecaster. It separates historical code search from deployment selection, where completed forecast windows supply the new feedback. Machine learning engineering agents. MLAgentBench (Huang et al., 2024) evaluates agents that read and write files, execute experiments, and inspect outputs. MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025) assesses model development and experimentation on machine learning competitions. AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025) searches over code solutions, while TabFM-Auto (Fu et al., 2026) focuses pipeline search around frozen tabular model. Our design shares the codeexecutionfeedback pattern, but couples pipeline adaptation with chronological feedback and strategy selection for repeated forecasting.

sections.title: B Pipeline Interface
sections.content: Four functions pass prepared data and state between pipeline stages. The first, preprocess, receives the observed history and task description and returns prepared data and local state. engineer constructs variables from these inputs. select_context creates one or more forecasting cases, specifying the histories and variable groups supplied to the foundation model. postprocess maps model outputs back to the target scale and returns point and quantile forecasts in the original target units. State is local to the current invocation. It can hold fitted transforms or auxiliary predictors derived from the available history. During deployment, these components may be fitted again on newly available history while their code remains fixed. The evaluator supplies the same chronological windows to all candidates. Candidate code receives no target values beyond each windows origin. The agent can access the labels of the adaptation windows through evaluation feedback; these labels are not passed to the pipeline as prediction inputs. Later selection feedback is used by the system only after code search finishes. All four functions and their evaluation records are retained so the agent can inspect earlier attempts.

sections.title: C Historical Selection Details
sections.content: The reference configuration describes each target using up to 96 recent observations and the reference median forecast. Its six features are: the latest value relative to the recent median; the mean of the last eight observations relative to the mean of the earlier half of the recent history; the first forecast relative to the latest observation; the mean forecast relative to the recent median; the standard deviation across the forecast horizon; and the last forecast relative to the first. Each feature is scaled by the recent historical standard deviation, with small floor for nearly constant series. At new origin, the selector first filters out windows whose outcomes are not yet complete. It uses records for the current item when at least three distinct origins are available; otherwise it pools the 7 available records. For each target, it standardizes the feature coordinates using the historical feature standard deviations, floored at 0.25. Distance is the mean squared difference in these coordinates. The selector retrieves up to 12 nearest records and gives each an initial weight of 1/(1 + d), where is this distance. Weights are then normalized within each origin before applying the weighted-error selection rule. For each candidate and historical window, the loss is its mean absolute scaled error (MASE) divided by the reference MASE, with denominator floor of 108. MASE divides mean absolute forecast error by the mean absolute seasonal difference in the history available at that origin. Candidate ranking before deployment uses mean selectionwindow MASE, with the quantile score as tiebreaker. The portable configuration retains three ranked candidates plus the reference if it is not already among them. Initial feedback comes from the completed adaptation and selection windows; subsequent completed forecasts extend this history. With no available feedback, the selector uses the reference pipeline.

sections.title: D Discovered Deployment Strategies
sections.content: These cases illustrate task-specific features, domain-informed representations, business rules, measurement structure, and auxiliary predictors. Tab. 2 compares seven example tasks with direct inference using the same frozen TimesFM 3.0 backbone. Each test score covers all official windows and targets of its task. Historical adaptation and selection scores are reported separately; the selected examples do not represent the aggregate benchmark result. D.1 Supply Chain: Learning When Demand Is Zero holiday can break an otherwise regular weekly pattern. On July 4, 2024, in the first official forecast window of Supply_Chain_Customer, the first customers observed order count is zero. The direct models median forecast is 195.23; TIMERSIs is zero. The agent writes date-based correction rather than general low-demand threshold. It checks past observations on July 4, Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Years Day. For each target, the correction requires at least four past holiday observations, of which at least 80% must be zero. When this condition holds, it sets all nine forecast quantiles to zero on the relevant holiday. Thus, calendar hypothesis becomes rule supported by that targets history. The agent also tests corrections for the day after holiday. Historical feedback leads it to restrict this adjustment to the day after July 4 rather than applying it to dates such as Black Friday. Further revisions align the normalized forecast shapes of orders, pieces, and revenue for the same customer. Tab. 3 shows all six revisions in this search. The main adaptation gain comes from the first holidayaware correction; later edits refine it. The task contains 36 targets and 12 windows of 30 days. On the four relevant holiday dates, all 144 target values are zero; direct inference predicts nonzero values, while TIMERSI predicts zero. Across all dates and targets, the complete pipeline reduces MASE by 6.70%, including its other corrections. D.2 Parking: Revising How the Model Uses the Calendar The task predicts available parking spaces every 15 minutes for the next week. Calendar information can describe more than change in average availability: the daily pattern may also differ between weekdays and weekends. The agent explores both using separate calendar predictor and supplying calendar features to TimesFM. Tab. 4 shows all six evaluated revisions. The first calendar-predictor blend increases adaptation error. The agent then removes its contribution and builds known-future calendar inputs instead. The selected program contains 22 features: daily and weekly sine and cosine terms, weekend and Saturday indicators, and weekendtime-of-day interactions. Features cover both historical and future timestamps. The program includes periodic feature only when the history spans at least 1.5 of its cycles. The chosen pipeline keeps the calendar predictors output weight at zero: the improvement comes from program that supplies new inputs to the frozen model. On the full test task of 354 car parks, MASE falls from 0.678730 to 0.641658 and CRPS from 0.046609 to 0.044105. Adaptation uses three origins and selection uses five, each with 32 car parks. Comparisons are within columns. Revision 4 is deployed, rather than the last revision or the adaptation winner. D.3 Ocean Currents: Using Tidal Knowledge in Model Inputs In current_velocity/10T/long, the agent uses known tidal periods to separate predictable oscillations from the remaining signal. Its program includes tidal constituents such as M2 (12.42 hours) and K1 (23.93 hours). It selects constituents whose frequencies can be distinguished over the available history and fits their amplitudes and phases for each target. Before applying the decomposition, historical backtest checks whether the tidal fit improves on constant-mean predictor. The program subtracts the fitted tidal component from the history, supplies the residual to TimesFM, and adds the extrapolated component back to the weekend = np.where(dow >= 5, 1., -1.) for in (1, 2, 3): phase = 2 * np.pi * * tod rows += [weekend * np.sin(phase), weekend * np.cos(phase)] Fig. 4: Calendar interactions in the generated program. The core feature code, condensed for readability. Here, tod is the fraction of day and dow ranges from Monday (0) to Sunday (6). These features cover both history and forecast dates. point and quantile forecasts. Thus, domain knowledge changes the models numerical input rather than only adding textual description. The selected pipeline reduces MASE from 0.871531 to 0.835129 (4.18%) and CRPS from 0.278207 to 0.276433 (0.64%). These scores cover ten series, six variables, and five official windows, each forecasting 432 ten-minute steps (72 hours). D.4 Solar: Respecting Daily-Reset Pattern In Australia_Solar, the agent identifies pattern consistent with daily-reset counter: values rise within the day, reach plateau, and reset. This observed structure motivates different correction from one designed for instantaneous power. The program estimates normalized daily profile s(h) from the previous 28 valid days. For each forecast day and quantile, it fits level to the model output and reconstructs the path as s(h). The correction preserves the historical daily shape and reset while using the model forecast to set the level. The agent also explores daily-total experts and seasonal profiles. Separate historical selection favors the simpler shape projection. The selected pipeline reduces MASE by 2.86% and CRPS by 2.66% across three targets and 35 official windows, each covering 72 hours. 9 D.5 Auto Production: Building Calendar-Aware Specialist the monthly seasonal-factor The official task Auto_Production_SF/M/short series contains RSF_AutoProduction, not vehicle production counts. The agent builds on calendar-aware predictor and explores holiday interactions, monthspecific trends, and reversible seasonal transformations. It uses historical forecasts to choose smoothing rate for each month, then shrinks these choices toward common default. The resulting specialist supplies the point forecast. TimesFMs quantile deviations and historical forecast errors inform the predictive distribution. This case illustrates the broader action space of deployment code: the agent can fit an auxiliary predictor, not only add input features. Across all five 12-month test windows, MASE falls from 0.756537 for direct inference to 0.233980 for TIMERSI, 69.07% reduction. The pipeline used to start the final search already achieves 0.313005; the six further revisions reduce its test MASE by 25.25%. These comparisons distinguish the complete deployment gain from the additional gain of that search. D.6 COVID Reports: Revising an Overextended Trend plausible first idea need not be the best program. On ECDC_COVID, the agent starts with reversible logarithmic transformation, but adaptation MASE increases from 3.9173 to 4.1816. It then examines past forecast errors and finds overly strong upward extrapolation in the cases it inspects. The next revision blends the model with damped trend predictor, lowering adaptation MASE to 2.9624. Further edits handle isolated reporting spikes and repeated values at the end of the history. The agent also tests shorter context and adjusts positive trend damping according to how long the recent growth has lasted. Tab. 5 gives the complete six-revision trace. The selected pipeline gives equal weight to the model and the auxiliary predictor in log space. Across nine countries and five 30-day test windows, it reduces task-level MASE by 7.91% and CRPS by 15.62%. These are aggregate gains across the task, not improvements in every country or window. Revision Direct TimesFM 1. Log transformation 2. Damped trend blend 3. Repeated-value handling 4. Shorter context 5. Growth-duration damping 6. Milder damping and blend Adaptation 3.9173 4.1816 2.9624 2.7920 2.7604 2.7252 2.8398 Selection 5.0403 4.2079 3.8822 4.1122 4.1589 4.1114 3.7878 Tab. 5: COVID-report MASE on separate historical sets. Selection favors revision 6, which uses milder damping, over revision 5, which has the lowest adaptation error. D.7 Atmospheric Variables: Separating the Daily Cycle NE_China_Wind forecasts four atmospheric variables, including wind components, geopotential height, and temperature. The agent fits daily harmonics in overlapping historical segments, allowing their amplitudes to change over time. It subtracts the estimated cycle, lets TimesFM forecast the remaining signal, and restores the future cycle afterward. The transformation is reversible and fitted from the available history. The selected program reduces MASE by 2.22% across all four variables and 30 official 24-hour windows.

sections.title: E Benchmark Protocol and Full Results
sections.content: Evaluation scope. TIME provides 98 dataset frequencyhorizon tasks from 50 datasets, covering 111,177 forecast instances. FEV-bench provides 100 tasks; our results cover all 1,308 specified forecast windows and 235,039 forecast instances. One instance is one serieswindowtarget combination. We follow the released task definitions, including their target columns, sampling frequencies, horizons, forecast origins, and seasonal periods. All target variables and test windows contribute to each tasks score. Available covariates retain their official roles: past-only covariates stop at the forecast origin, while known-future covariates may extend across the horizon. Pipeline configuration. The default backbone is TimesFM 3.0. Its weights stay fixed throughout search and deployment. Our default code agent is Claude Code (Claude Fable 5). The frozen candidate archive also includes programs developed with Claude Opus 5. Agents can use task and variable descriptions, timestamps, observed values, and available covariates. The editable stages are listed in App. B; the historical selector is specified in App. C.
